description: We are passionate IT students interested in AI, software development, data science, and space exploration. Our team has experience in national and international hackathons. We aim to develop innovative solutions using NASA's open data. We welcome creative and collaborative teammates with skills in AI/ML, data science, UI/UX, web development, astronomy, or space science. Let's build something impactful together!
summary: Trend Detective is a web app that answers one question with NASA data: is a place really changing, or is it just the usual year-to-year wobble? Users spin a 3D globe and click any spot, pick one of Malaysia's 16 states and territories, or type a plain question such as "Is Penang getting rainier?". The app fetches monthly NASA POWER data (MERRA-2, CERES) from 1981 for 18 variables, including temperature, rain, soil moisture, haze and sea temperature. It runs two trend tests, Mann-Kendall with Sen's slope and a least-squares t-test, both adjusted for year-to-year memory so they do not raise false alarms. The answer is one plain sentence: what is changing, how fast per decade, and whether it is statistically significant, with a chart and how many more years would be needed to tell. Trend maps test every grid cell around a place, or the whole globe, and timelapse, wind and satellite layers add context. Guided stories, a tour, Bahasa Malaysia and a plain-words explainer make it easy for students. Our statistics match SciPy and an independent Python check on real data (216 of 216 cases). This matters because one hot year or a viral post is easy to mistake for a trend; Trend Detective lets anyone test a claim with real evidence in under a minute.
details:
Try it: https://yc-lim12.github.io/trend-detective/

Code: https://github.com/Yc-Lim12/trend-detective

Submission files (Google Drive folder: poster, project document, 3–5 min video, 30 s demo):

https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1PdE_sgo5Obk54tw4cwKGOrdJEwNNPG3U?usp=sharing

What it does

Trend Detective helps anyone check whether a place's climate is really changing or just going through normal ups and downs. A single hot year, a flood or a viral post often gets mistaken for a trend. We wanted a tool that answers that question honestly, with NASA data and real statistics, in under a minute.

A user starts in one of four ways:

- clicking any spot on a 3D globe or flat map;

- choosing one of Malaysia's 16 states and federal territories, or a region such as Borneo;

- typing a plain question in English or Bahasa Malaysia, such as "Is Penang getting rainier in December?";

- answering three short questions in the "Help me choose" guide.

The app sets up a "case file" and gives a verdict in one sentence: what is changing, how fast per decade, and whether it is statistically significant. If it is not significant, it says how many more years of data would be needed to tell.

How it works

- Data: monthly NASA POWER data from 1981 for 18 variables: air, day and night temperature, ground temperature, rain, evaporation, soil moisture, humidity, water vapour, sunlight, cloud, haze, wind, pressure, ozone, sea surface temperature and snow.

- Areas: one grid cell, a box of 2° to 20°, or a whole region. Boxes over 10° are fetched in parts. A Malaysian state uses its real boundary: each NASA grid cell is weighted by how much of it lies inside the state. Moving the area slider turns the state into a square box around it.

- Statistics: each case runs two tests, Mann-Kendall with Sen's slope and a least-squares t-test. Both are adjusted for year-to-year memory (autocorrelation), which otherwise makes trends look more certain than they are.

- Chart: a 95% confidence band, a change-point test, an optional 1991–2020 baseline, a 5-year average, and a projection "if the trend continues".

- Seasons: users can test the whole year, a season or one month, or every month with the seasonal cycle removed.

Map layers:

- Trend map: tests every grid cell around a place, or the whole globe, and corrects for testing many cells at once (false discovery rate).

- Opposite-trend finder: points out where one part of an area is rising while another falls.

- Timelapse: plays every month.

- Rain now: NASA GPM IMERG.

- Wind: animated particles that follow NASA POWER's average 10 m wind, coloured by wind speed.

- Whole world: NASA's global monthly maps, shown as "difference from normal".

Extras:

- Compare two places on one chart.

- Scan all 18 variables for one place.

- A "spike, not trend" warning.

- Data-quality notes on missing years.

- CSV download and shareable links.

- A plain-words explainer (built in, or AI with the user's own key).

Benefits and intended impact

- Students learn what "statistically significant" means by testing their own town, not a textbook example.

- Teachers get ready-made guided stories: city heat in Kuala Lumpur, haze, east versus west coast monsoon rain, a warming sea, and wildfire smoke in Wisconsin.

- Everyone can check a climate claim against real evidence before sharing it.

- Malaysian users can explore every state in their own language. The app also works for any place on Earth.

Our goal is fewer misleading claims in both directions: fewer "it's just one hot year" dismissals, and fewer "this proves climate change" posts built on a single spike.

Tools and technology

Website: HTML, CSS and JavaScript (no framework), D3.js and TopoJSON. A WebGL2 shader draws the globe and flat map, with sun lighting and NASA satellite imagery.

NASA data and services:

- NASA POWER API: MERRA-2; CERES SYN1deg, from 2001, for sunlight, cloud and haze;

- NASA GIBS: Blue Marble, daily VIIRS true colour from NOAA-20, GPM IMERG rain;

- NASA Goddard SVS cloud imagery;

- NASA Giovanni, used to cross-check our data.

Other data: Malaysian state boundaries from geoBoundaries (© OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL).

Checking our maths:

- Python (NumPy, SciPy) re-checks 552 numbers from our statistics code against SciPy; all match.

- An independent Python pipeline compares all 18 variables at 6 test places on real NASA data: 216 of 216 cases match.

- Cross-checked against NASA Giovanni: at the MERRA-2 grid point 3.0°N, 101.25°E (Klang Valley, west of Kuala Lumpur), all 540 months of air temperature from 1981 to 2025 agree with Giovanni's MERRA-2 values (median difference 0.006 °C), and the 45-year trend is the same (+0.186 °C per decade).

- A simulation of trend-free monthly data shows the memory adjustment cuts false alarms from 29% to 5%.

- Automated Node.js tests cover the question parser, the data handling and the state weighting.

Development: Git and GitHub, one branch per team member.

Hardware: none. It runs in any modern browser on a laptop or phone.

How it is creative

- The "detective" framing: a case file, evidence tiles and a verdict turn statistics into an investigation students want to finish.

- Honest uncertainty: instead of stopping at "not significant", the app says how many more years would be needed to tell.

- Real-shape state averages: Malaysian states use their real boundaries, not rough rectangles.

- Data and imagery side by side: pictures are labelled as pictures and data as data, so users don't confuse them.

Factors our team considered

Statistical honesty:

- year-to-year memory;

- testing many map cells at once;

- two satellite datasets that don't match where they join in 2001, so sunlight and cloud cover start in 2001;

- NASA POWER's soil value over the open ocean, which is a placeholder rather than a measurement.

Resolution: NASA POWER cells are about 50 km wide, so the app says when a place is smaller than one cell.

Access:

- two languages;

- works on phones;

- keyboard and screen-reader support;

- reduced-motion mode;

- light and dark themes.

Speed: NASA answers are cached in the browser, so revisiting a place, month or variable needs no new download.

Credit: every data source is cited in the in-app Methods page.

Use of AI

Our team planned and solved the challenge ourselves. We chose the problem, the NASA datasets, the statistical methods and the structure of the app, and made every design and content decision. AI tools only assisted us; they did not choose, plan or solve the challenge.

We used Claude (Anthropic) and ChatGPT (OpenAI) as AI coding assistants to help write and review code. In the app, "Explain this simply" and "Ask AI" use a built-in explainer by default: it runs in the browser, uses no AI and sends nothing. Only if a user enters their own OpenAI or Google Gemini API key can they ask for a longer AI explanation or ask follow-up questions; the case's numbers are then sent to that service. All trend tests and numbers are computed by our own code from NASA data, not by AI.

Videos: our team wrote the scripts and voiceover, directed every revision, and did the final cut and assembly. All statistics shown come from our application's own code and real NASA data. We used Claude (Anthropic) to help produce the demo video's motion graphics: the scripted screen recording of our real website, the camera moves, the on-screen titles and highlights, the animated chart reveal, the space backdrop, the sound effects and the Trend Detective logo. The website footage is a real recording of our working application and was not altered. No measurements, charts or maps were generated or changed by AI. The voiceover is recorded by a team member and is not synthetic. No NASA logos or branding appear in AI-assisted content.

Background music is not AI-generated: 'Disco Wheel' by Mood Maze on Uppbeat (https://uppbeat.io/c/mood-maze), license code RTIDIQTCMN29HGE9.
